body.cap: WiseJet set up its first standalone booth at CES 2025 and has since exhibited for two consecutive years through 2026, with a CES 2027 booth also planned. Year after year, the company leaves its mark on the global stage, steadily building the presence of its 'Zero-Delay Wireless' technology. | Courtesy of WiseJet

body.x: As the Physical AI era gathers pace, a new bottleneck has surfaced. For robots, autonomous vehicles and extended-reality (XR) devices to see, judge and move on their own, they must exchange vast amounts of video and data without interruption — and without delay. Yet cables run into the physical limits of rotation, detachment and space, while Wi-Fi is held back by compression and latency. The company driving into that gap with a 60GHz millimeter-wave (mmWave) wireless chipset is WiseJet Inc. (CEO Chulsoon Park).

Founded in 2015 by Chulsoon Park, a former professor at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), WiseJet is a fabless company developing chipsets that use the unlicensed 60GHz ultra-high-frequency band to replace conventional wired connectors and cables with wireless links. Its core message is simple: in an age when AI descends into the physical world, WiseJet realizes that connection "wirelessly."
"The technology risk has been removed" — Trust built on investment and exhibition momentum

WiseJet raised KRW 5 billion (approx. US$3.6 million) in a Pre-Series B round this June. Five investors took part, including ES Investor, Ecopro Partners, Muir Woods Ventures, NBH Capital and D&D. The round brings WiseJet's cumulative funding to KRW 14 billion (approx. US$10 million). Previously, in its March 2023 Series A, the company secured KRW 4.8 billion from L&S Venture Capital, Daedeok Venture Partners, Daesung Private Equity, Shinhan Capital and the Korea SMEs and Startups Agency.

The new capital serves as a "stepping stone" toward mass production: preparing the near-field wireless connector chip "WC6" for production, converting the video-transmission chip "WV6" to an application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC), and expanding the R&D team.

The company aims to ramp up full-scale production of both chips over the second half of this year and next, while mapping a roadmap toward a 2028 technology-based special listing in step with follow-on rounds.

Apart from fundraising, WiseJet has steadily accumulated exposure on the global stage. At CES 2025, its standalone booth at the Las Vegas Convention Center showcased a robot-joint wireless solution and 8K/60Hz wireless video transmission, drawing visits from more than 110 companies — of which some 50 global robotics and home-appliance firms moved on to follow-up discussions. At CES 2026, it demonstrated DisplayPort (DP) video transmitted wirelessly over 10 meters, and a CES 2027 booth is already secured in an LVCC hall, extending the run to three consecutive years. A Tokyo IT exhibition is also on the calendar for the second half of this year.

In short, WiseJet's current stage is not about proving whether the technology works, but about moving proven technology into the capital-intensive phase of mass production. The WV6 video chip has already completed development on an FPGA (field-programmable gate array) basis and awaits only ASIC conversion. The remaining question is execution and volume, not technical uncertainty.

body.cap: WiseJet's near-field wireless connector chip "WC6," shown as an eDP-applied prototype (WC6-AiP-eDPv0.1). A wireless module takes the place of the connector slot where a cable once plugged in. | Courtesy of WiseJet

body.x: "WC6 erases the 'connector,' WV6 erases the 'delay' — two pillars of a cable-free world"

WiseJet's core weapons in wireless transmission are two chips. One eliminates the physical "slot" where a cable used to plug in; the other eliminates latency, the chronic weakness of wireless. Their names are similar, but their roles are entirely different.

WC6 — the cable-free "wireless connector." WC6 (Wireless Connector) wirelessizes not the cable itself but the connector into which a cable plugs. Hold two devices within tens of millimeters of each other and data flows at 10Gbps. Where competing products top out at around 6Gbps, that is nearly double the speed — and, given that video transmission generally requires 8 to 10Gbps, it is the very threshold that decides whether a chip can be applied to video at all. On top of that comes a latency of 7 nanoseconds (ns); one nanosecond is one billionth of a second.

That is roughly the time light travels a little over 2 meters, so users cannot even sense whether the link is wireless or wired. With no physical contact point, there is no wear, no contact failure, no contamination. It turns domains that "only worked on contact" — robot joints spinning endlessly through 360 degrees, or display-inspection lines that press pogo pins onto each panel — into domains that "work without contact."

WV6 — the "wireless video" with neither stutter nor compression. WV6 (Wireless Video) is a video-streaming chip that sends 4K and 8K ultra-high-definition images over up to 10 meters with latency under 1ms. Its differentiator is "full, no-compression" transmission.

The reason mirroring a smartphone to a TV at home stutters and blurs is that Wi-Fi compresses the video before sending it. WV6 sends the image intact, without compression, so there is no quality loss; its beamforming steers around obstacles and blocks interference, so the picture holds steady even under heavy data load. Sending ultra-high-definition video wirelessly without any compression is a rare level of engineering worldwide, the company says. The 8K/60Hz and DisplayPort (DP) wireless transmissions shown at CES both belong to this line.

Why is this "zero latency" decisive? People notice on-screen lag once it exceeds 0.1 second. For a gamer it decides a win or loss; for an autonomous vehicle, the split second to read and react to traffic; in robotic surgery, exactly where the scalpel lands. In fields where a single beat of delay quickly becomes danger, wireless video transmission that reduces latency to virtually zero is not an option but a precondition.

body.cap: Key specifications of WC6: 10Gbps throughput, sub-7ns zero latency, 0.01–30cm near-field operation, 150mW low power, 4.6×4.8mm compact size, and multi-lane operation free of RF interference. | Courtesy of WiseJet

body.x: "Multi-lane and single-chip, at once" — WiseJet's claimed edge

The vision of wireless replacing cables is not new in itself. Standards such as WiGig and WirelessHD have existed for well over a decade but never cleared the wall of commercialization. WiseJet points to three areas where it says it differs from those earlier standards.

The first is zero-latency, fully uncompressed transmission. Where conventional wireless mirroring compresses data — inviting quality loss and stutter — WiseJet transmits video uncompressed and has all but eliminated delay. According to a comparison the company provided, WiGig-style video latency runs around 21ms, while WiseJet has cut it to near zero. The company cites same-band rivals Qualcomm and Peraso (in the 20ms range) and Sibeam (5ms), arguing that its video chip is ahead on the numbers.[^1]

The second is "multi-lane." Most competing products stay on a single channel (1×1) because of RF interference. WiseJet says its proprietary beamforming-based interference-blocking technology enables multi-lane configurations of 4, 8 and 16 lanes, securing an effective transmission speed of up to 180Gbps. "WiseJet is currently the only company to implement 10Gbps multi-lane and a single-chip solution at the same time," the company states. These comparative figures, however, rest on company-provided data; third-party verification against mass-production products is still under way.

The third is timing. Unlike the 2010s, when wireless video transmission was a "nice-to-have," today — when autonomous driving and humanoid robots must recognize and react to video in real time — ultra-low-latency, high-reliability wireless transmission has become a "must-have" piece of infrastructure.

body.cap: CEO Chulsoon Park (second from right) explains WiseJet's wireless video transmission technology to a global buyer visiting the booth. | Courtesy of WiseJet

body.x: "Not a choice but an inevitability"… CEO Chulsoon Park on what lies beyond mass production​​​​​​​
In person, CEO Chulsoon Park repeatedly stressed that WiseJet's technology is not a "nice-to-have" option.

"There are fields that simply have no choice but to go wireless. A prime example is large LED signage," Park said, adding that "replacing the cabling that ties countless panels together with wireless modules makes installation far freer — and, crucially, the cost is almost the same as existing cable." The moment the assumption that wireless is more expensive breaks down, he argues, adoption is only a matter of time.
"If the price is the same, there's no reason to cling to cable. LED is going this way, no question."

Asked about applications, he turned first to the medical field. "Robotic operating rooms are packed with cables. Going wireless cuts the wiring and lowers contamination risk. When a surgeon watches a screen while cutting, even a fraction of a second's lag can mean touching the wrong spot — our technology has almost no delay, so it reduces that risk."

He added that the company has also built wireless, portable versions of ENT endoscopes and dental 3D oral scanners. Display-panel inspection follows the same logic. "Right now you press pogo pins onto each panel to check the signal, and there are an enormous number of panels. If you can pick up the signal wirelessly as they pass by, you can drop it straight into high-volume inspection equipment."

Asked where the technology peaks, he pointed to "full no-compression." "Sending ultra-high-definition video wirelessly without compressing it is uncommon even globally. Compression introduces delay and quality loss — we solved both at once, combining no-compression with beamforming that also handles interference."

So when does mass production come? Park raised the term "single run." "A fabless company has no factory, so it entrusts chip fabrication to an outside foundry. The stage where only our volume is dedicated and fabricated is what we call a single run. Our roadmap targets reaching that single run this year."

Still, reaching mass production of the WV6 chip will take more capital — his candid assessment. "We have to actually mass-produce and show stability and performance directly; that's how you persuade the next customer and the next investor. That's why follow-on investment matters."

Indeed, earlier this year a global display company and an aerospace company took WiseJet's chips into proof-of-concept (PoC) evaluations. The names cannot yet be disclosed, but the weight of the parties running the tests speaks for itself. What remains is to carry that validation through to an actual design-win.

body.cap: WiseJet executives and staff pose for a commemorative photo at the company's CES 2026 booth. CEO Chulsoon Park is at center. | Courtesy of WiseJet

body.x: Throughout the interview, Park kept returning to one word: "connection." "Engineering research can't end at papers or patents. It has to become an actual product that delivers value to people." In an era when AI grows ever more tightly bound to reality, he said, "WiseJet will realize that connection in the form of 'wireless,'" adding a pledge to "tie people, devices and the world into one." WiseJet holds 36 patents, and 18 of its 21 employees are R&D staff, more than a third of them master's- and doctoral-degree holders from KAIST and other science-and-technology institutes, Seoul National University and Yonsei University.

Ultimately, where WiseJet now stands is not a stage of proving the technology's excellence, but of deciding when and where to apply it. The performance is already validated; the remaining variable is the timetable for mass production and adoption. The follow-on investment that will turn a dedicated production run — the single run — into reality is the next gate.
